title: Correcting the modulus switch error in TFHE bootstrapping for real-valued computation
abstract:
Torus Fully Homomorphic Encryption (TFHE) enables the homomorphic
evaluation of arbitrary functions via Programmable Bootstrapping
(PBS). However, the modulus switching step inherent to bootstrapping
introduces a rounding error that forces the discretization of the
input space, limiting the achievable precision on real-valued inputs.
We propose a correction algorithm based on a first-order Taylor
expansion, applied after bootstrapping, that directly mitigates this
rounding error. Our method leverages the many-LUT technique to
simultaneously recover encryptions of the function and its derivative
within a single PBS, making the correction essentially free in terms
of bootstrapping latency. We support our construction with a
heuristic average-case noise analysis, validated by empirical
measurements, and demonstrate a tenfold reduction in bootstrapping
noise standard deviation. As a proof of concept, we apply our method
to the numerical integration of ordinary differential equations under
encryption.

      Abstract. Torus Fully Homomorphic Encryption (TFHE) enables the homomorphic
      evaluation of arbitrary functions via Programmable Bootstrapping (PBS). However,
      the modulus switching step inherent to bootstrapping introduces a rounding error
      that forces the discretization of the input space, limiting the achievable precision on
      real-valued inputs. We propose a correction algorithm based on a first-order Taylor
      expansion, applied after bootstrapping, that directly mitigates this rounding error.
      Our method leverages the many-LUT technique to simultaneously recover encryptions
      of the function and its derivative within a single PBS, making the correction essentially
      free in terms of bootstrapping latency. We support our construction with a heuristic
      average-case noise analysis, validated by empirical measurements, and demonstrate a
      tenfold reduction in bootstrapping noise standard deviation. As a proof of concept,
      we apply our method to the numerical integration of ordinary differential equations
      under encryption.
      Keywords: TFHE · Modulus switch · Numerical Integration · Taylor Expansion


1     Introduction
Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation over encrypted data without
decrypting them. Several schemes have been proposed in order to efficiently perform
homomorphic computation. All four schemes: TFHE [CGGI18, CGGI16], BFV [Bra12,
FV12], BGV [BGV14] and CKKS [CKKS17], rely on lattice-based cryptography, more
specifically on the Learning With Errors (LWE) cryptosystem and its refinement with
the Ring Learning With Errors (RLWE) [LPR13, SSTX09]. Each scheme was designed
for a specific purpose: BFV and BGV for integer modular arithmetic, TFHE for small
integer and boolean operations, and CKKS for approximate real number arithmetic. While
CKKS natively supports computations on real-valued numbers, it estimates functions using
polynomial expansions, which restricts the class of computable functions. On the other
hand, TFHE offers a versatile framework for operating on encrypted data via Programmable
Bootstrapping (PBS), enabling the homomorphic evaluation of arbitrary functions – at
the cost of requiring the plaintext space to be discretized, which bounds the achievable
precision.
    In this work, we explore an original positioning: performing approximate homomorphic
computation over real numbers, in the spirit of CKKS, but within the TFHE framework.
Such a combination is attractive, as it would associate the native real-valued arithmetic
of approximate schemes with the ability of TFHE to evaluate arbitrary – possibly non-
polynomial – functions through its Programmable Bootstrapping. Yet, this direction has
remained essentially unexplored, due to a fundamental obstacle: the bootstrapping of

2                                           Correcting the modulus switch error in TFHE


TFHE involves a modulus switching step, whose rounding error forces the quantization
of the input space. This error is harmless when TFHE is used, as originally designed,
on small integers or Boolean values, but it becomes the dominant obstacle as soon as
one aims at precise computation over real-valued inputs. Let us stress that our approach
does not target this classical setting, where redundancy in the test polynomial absorbs
the modulus switch error and the bootstrapping serves as a noise-reduction step. In our
regime, the bootstrapping instead serves to evaluate nonlinear functions on real-valued
ciphertexts, and the modulus switch error is an unavoidable approximation cost that we
seek to minimize.
    We propose to overcome this limitation with a correction algorithm that directly
mitigates the modulus switching error. Instead of reducing the rounding error of the
modulus switch eM S in the input space of the LUT – as done in prior works – our correction
operates in the output space: the LUT is evaluated at the perturbed point x0 = x + eM S ,
and we homomorphically reconstruct f (x) through the first-order Taylor approximation
f (x0 ) − eM S f ′ (x0 ), which requires the function being evaluated to be differentiable. To
compute this correction efficiently, our method leverages the many-LUT technique to
simultaneously recover encryptions of the function and its derivative within a single PBS,
making the correction essentially free in terms of bootstrapping latency.

Related Work
Both the GINX [CGGI18, CGGI16] and AP [LMK+ 23] bootstrapping algorithms perform
a modulus switching from a modulus q to 2N , where N is the Look-Up Table (LUT)
degree. Its rounding noise ultimately forces the quantization of the input space. Previous
works have addressed this limitation through several strategies.
    A first line of work [CLOT21, BBR26] focuses on making bootstrapping tractable for
large LUTs, thereby increasing the number of representable values and refining the input
space over which the PBS operates. A second line of work [BCL+ 25, ML20, KO22, LMP22,
BBB+ 23] encodes large-bit messages into multiple smaller sub-messages and builds efficient
arithmetic algorithms on top of these decompositions. While effective, both strategies come
at a significant computational cost: the former increases the bootstrapping complexity
through larger polynomial degrees, while the latter requires multiple bootstrappings to
evaluate a single function.
    A third line of work reduces the modulus switching error itself, prior to the blind
rotate: the collapse technique [CKLM24, ZYL+ 18] merges several CMUX steps within
the bootstrapping, while the mean compensation [dRDV26] corrects the expectation of
the rounding error. In contrast, our algorithm corrects this error after the blind rotate
operation.
    Recent works have also begun extending PBS-style functional evaluation to
CKKS [BCKS24, BKSS24, AKP25], enabling the homomorphic evaluation of non-
polynomial functions within the CKKS framework; however, these approaches currently
operate on bits or small-integer plaintext spaces, and do not support continuous real-valued
inputs.

Remark 1 (Security of approximate FHE schemes). Like the CKKS scheme, the present
scheme operates in the IND-CPAD security model rather than standard IND-CPA, due to
the approximate nature of decryption [LM21]. This means that an adversary with access to
a decryption oracle could in principle exploit the residual noise to recover information about
the secret key – the so-called Li-Micciancio attack. Standard mitigations, such as noise
flooding prior to decryption, apply directly and restore IND-CPAD security. Moreover,
the primary target applications of the present work – numerical computation and applied
mathematics – naturally operate in a compute-only server-side setting, where the server
never decrypts and the client decrypts its own results in a trusted environment. In this
context, the adversarial decryption oracle assumed by the attack is simply not available.

2.2.1    Noise estimation model
Throughout this work, we estimate noise growth using a standard average-case approach
based on the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), following the methodologies of [CGGI18].
Concretely, we model the coefficients of each noise polynomial as i.i.d. normal random
variables, so that noise variances propagate additively and can be tracked via a single
scalar at each step. This heuristic model is well-established in the FHE literature and has
been shown to give tighter and more representative estimates than worst-case subgaussian
bounds, see e.g. [CLP20, MP24] where the errors for BGV and BFV schemes are studied.
We use it as a supporting tool to dimension our method, and complement it with direct
empirical measurements over 10000 trials in Section 4 to validate its practical accuracy.

2.3     Programmable Bootstrapping (PBS)
Starting from the definitions recalled in the previous subsection, we can now define
programmable bootstrapping as the operation that takes LWEns (x) as input and returns
a ciphertext LWEs̄N (f (x)) where f is an arbitrary function. In the rest of this work, we
assume that x ∈ [− 14 + δ, 14 − δ] with δ > 0 satisfying δ ≫ ∥einit + eM S ∥, so as to ensure
that the bootstrapping output does not overflow the torus in the case of non-periodic
functions.


2.3.1    The classical programmable bootstrapping

Let us first present the standard programmable bootstrapping. Usually, PBS consists of
four phases: (1) a key switching that moves the input ciphertext from being encrypted
under a key of size N – the RLWE polynomial degree – down to a smaller LWE key of
dimension n, (2) a modulus switching, (3) a blind rotate that homomorphically rotates a
test polynomial, (4) a sample extract.
    Our contribution focuses on mitigating the noise introduced during the modulus
switching, which is in most of the case the largest noise. Thus, we omit in the rest of this
work the initial key switching and consider initially an LWEns (x) as (a0 , ..., an−1 , b) under
a secret key (s0 , ..., sn−1 ). We denote einit as the initial noise of this encryption.

4     Experiments

In this section, we present three experimental studies. In the first one, we perform general
purpose PBS, taking sigmoid and tanh functions as examples. On top of this, we compare
the performance of classical PBS and our correction method for ciphertext/ciphertext
multiplication of real-valued numbers. Last, we carry out the numerical integration of a
toy one-dimensional ODE. All experiments were conducted with an NVIDIA H100 GPU.

4.3    Numerical Integration of ODEs
In this last subsection, we compute ODE numerical integration with encrypted initial
coordinates. Encrypted scientific computing has recently been explored in [KPSL25], where
the CKKS scheme is used to solve linear PDEs via finite difference schemes. To the best of

investigated in previous work. We believe that this use case might have applications in
industrial setups, for instance where different parties wish to perform numerical simulations
and where one party has the initial coordinates and another has the numerical formula to
solve the ODE. Nonetheless, numerical integration requires high precision, motivating the
use of our Taylor correction algorithm.

5    Conclusion
We have presented a Taylor-based correction algorithm that enables homomorphic compu-
tation over real numbers within the TFHE framework. By performing a first-order Taylor
expansion to mitigate the modulus switch error, our method achieves a tenfold reduction
in bootstrapping noise at negligible computational overhead, as confirmed by both our
theoretical noise analysis and experimental results on sigmoid, tanh, and LWE/LWE mul-
tiplication. The agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical measurements
validates the relevance of our noise model. As a proof of concept, we have demonstrated
that homomorphic numerical integration of ODEs is achievable, a use case that, to the
best of our knowledge, has not been previously investigated.
    Several directions for future work naturally arise. First, our algorithm can be extended
to a second-order Taylor expansion, at the cost of additional parameters, which may further
reduce the truncation error for highly irregular functions. Second, the combination of our
real-number encoding with multivariate function evaluation opens perspectives toward
more complex numerical workflows in the encrypted domain.
